rows.etymology: 9. Bng. uśia ‘little, a little bit’, Deog. iśi ‘ditto’, Rp. usu ‘few, a little bit’ cannot derive < OIA *occha- ‘small, thin, mean’ (2540) because of Bng. oiċhɔ ‘vain, conceited’, whereas uśia and iśi correspond semantically exactly to thoṛa/o which is used in other surrounding dialects (cf. H. thoṛā ‘little’). I therefore assume that Turner has mingled here two actually separate lemmata, one meaning *‘little’ and the other *‘mean’. The meaning *‘little’ is in addition only found in Pal. úču ‘few, a little’, Klm. ätuši H ‘a little’ (prefixed with a demonstrative as also found in äthã̄ ‘this’) and učuṭ HL ‘few, a little’, Ash. ūċuk ‘a little’, Dm. ú̄čha, ú̄ča ‘little’, Rāj. ušɛr ‘little’ (Z.), Kalk. učuṭ ‘little’ (Z.), Kal. učˈīk ‘light (of weight)’, Bashg. ačok ‘some, a little’, and possibly Tor. ašùr ‘a little’ and in Kamd. e čˈa ‘a few’ and ˈe cok ‘a little’, and also Garh. ucchi, ichi ‘(just) a little’. All other NIA languages have by and large only the meaning *‘mean’, and therefore the origin for the words meaning ‘little’ has to be a different one. The loss of the closure in the Bng., Deog. and other words must have taken place before the start of depalatalisation.
